newsitem.title: ISRAEL: U.S. envoy Ross expects Hebron deal shortly.
newsitem.headline: U.S. envoy Ross expects Hebron deal shortly.

text.p: U.S. envoy Dennis Ross said before leaving the Middle East on Wednesday that he expected Israel and the Palestinians to reach a Hebron deal after he returned to the region next week.
Ross met Palestinian President Yasser Arafat in the West Bank town of Ramallah before heading for the airport as Israeli and Palestinian negotiators ended a further day of talks.

"I will be giving a positive report to President Clinton and I will be returning here no later than Monday particularly because the work is going very well and because I hope and expect that we will conclude an agreement shortly thereafter," Ross told reporters.
In Hebron, Israeli troops scuffled with Jewish settlers opposed to any withdwrawal from the volatile town.

Witnesses said police arrested about 20 settlers after an illegal pre-dawn attempt to take over two vacant houses in Hebron's Arab casbah. They said settlers hurled eggs, apples and stones at Israeli soldiers.
Hebron's Jews are angry about moves towards towards a long-overdue Israeli transfer of 80 percent of the town holy to Moslems and Jews to Arafat's Palestinian Authority.

Ross said he was "very pleased with the progress that had been made" and was leaving members of his staff behind to continue mediation efforts between Israelis and Palestinians to resolve final disputes blocking Israel's withdrawal.
Arafat told reporters: "We hope that we will have this agreement for the implementation of what had been agreed upon very soon."
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's policy adviser Dore Gold told Israel Radio earlier that there was still work to be done.

Hebron, taken by Israel with the rest of the West Bank in the 1967 Middle East war, is the last Palestinian town due for self-rule under a 1995 peace deal. Israel's security fears have delayed its transfer.

Hebron's settlers feel betrayed by Netanyahu, a rightist backer of Jewish settlement in occupied lands who has nonetheless promised to uphold the Hebron deal signed by the left-leaning government he ousted in May.
An Israeli rabbi accused Netanyahu of breaking a written election promise to the ultra-orthodox Habad movement never to cede land to the Arabs.

In the autonomous Gaza Strip, Jewish settlers laid a ceremonial cornerstone for what they said would be a new neighbourhood in the Israeli-ruled enclave of Netzarim in reaction to the planned opening of road near the settlement to Palestinian traffic.
Palestinian security officials said the road, closed to Arab traffic after an Islamist suicide bomber on a bicycle blew himself up on it in 1994, would be reopened on Thursday.
The road had been restricted to use by the Israeli army, Jewish settlers and Palestinian police and dignitaries.

Israel turned over most of the Gaza Strip to Palestinian self-rule in 1994 but retained control of Jewish settlements there. About 3,000 Jews live amid one million Palestinians in the impoverished territory.
The fate of the Jews in Gaza, Hebron and in other West Bank settlements will be decided in "final-status" talks between Israel and the Palestinians due to be completed by May 1999.
